problem.text: How many positive integers less than or equal to $240$ can be expressed as a sum of distinct factorials? Consider $0!$ and $1!$ to be distinct.

steps.title: Where to start: list the factorials you can use
steps.body: Factorials grow very fast, so only a handful of them can appear in a sum up to $240$. List them first: $0! = 1$, $1! = 1$, $2! = 2$, $3! = 6$, $4! = 24$, $5! = 120$. The next one, $6! = 720$, is already far too big.

your_turn.prompt: What is the largest sum you can make using each of these six factorials at most once? Does the limit of $240$ ever get in the way?
your_turn.answer: $1 + 1 + 2 + 6 + 24 + 120 = 154$. That is below $240$, so every possible sum is allowed.

steps.title: The small factorials can repeat values
steps.body: Careful: $0!$ and $1!$ are both $1$, and $0! + 1! = 2!$. So different choices of the small factorials $1, 1, 2$ can give the same total, and we must count totals, not choices. Split the problem into a small part (from $0!, 1!, 2!$) and a big part (from $3!, 4!, 5!$).

your_turn.prompt: Which totals can you make from $1, 1, 2$ if you may also use none of them?

steps.title: The big factorials never collide
steps.body: Each of $6$, $24$, $120$ is either in the sum or not, which gives $2 \cdot 2 \cdot 2 = 8$ big parts: $0, 6, 24, 30, 120, 126, 144, 150$. Any two of these differ by at least $6$, while the small part only adds $0$ to $4$.

your_turn.prompt: Why can two different (big part, small part) pairs never give the same number?
your_turn.answer: Two big parts differ by at least $6$, but small parts differ by at most $4$, so the gap can never be closed.

steps.title: Put it together
steps.body: Every pair of a big part and a small part gives a different number, so there are $8 \cdot 5 = 40$ totals. One of them is $0$ (use nothing at all), which is not positive, so we remove it: $40 - 1 = 39$. The answer is **39**.
